Regulation of location, size, and features of signs is necessary to: 1) enable the public to locate goods, services, and facilities without difficulty, 2) improve the attractiveness of the Town, and 3) protect property values. This Division is to avoid content-based regulation, and instead to regulate time, place and manner. More communication is desirable during elections, so citizens may freely express their viewpoints, and therefore this allows increased opportunities for signs during these periods, without limiting content. At all times, any sign permitted can carry any legal message, political or not, commercial or not. However, it is not the intent of this Article that all signs are built to the maximum size. The Town encourages use of the minimum signage necessary to meet the purposes. The Town establishes regulations to: 1. Promote and protect the public health, safety, and general welfare; 2. Protect the character of historic areas and residential neighborhoods; 3. Enhance the economy of the Town by promoting reasonable, orderly and effective display of signs; 4. Restrict signs and lights which increase clutter or the probability of traffic accidents by obstructing vision; 5. Promote signs compatible with their surroundings. It is the objective hereof to protect the aesthetic, cultural, and historic qualities of the Town, which are unique and vital to the Town's interest, to ensure these are not compromised. This is done by regulating the number, size, placement, installation and maintenance of signs. The fact that signs are intended to command visual contact, grants to signs a proportionally greater role than other structures in determining the aesthetic quality of the Town. Signs can detract from the beauty of the Town and lower property values. The aesthetic impact of signs has an economic factor that can bear heavily upon enjoyment and value of property; therefore, regulation of signs is validly justified on the basis of conserving property value and encouraging the most appropriate use of land throughout the Town. It is both rational and important for citizens to plan their physical surroundings so unsightliness is minimized. To comply with Federal and Georgia law, the Town has determined the following: large billboards are, as the U.S. Supreme Court has recognized, an aesthetic harm; the Georgia Supreme Court has upheld sign regulations on the basis of aesthetics and preserving the beauty of environment; and, judicial decisions of the Federal Eleventh Circuit have recognized that portable signs are visual clutter and a potential traffic hazard. These holdings support the constitutionality hereof. With these purposes in mind, it is the intention hereof to authorize the use of signs that:

25 Are compatible with their surroundings, legible, appropriate to the type of activity to which they pertain, and expressive of the identity of the individual properties or of the Town as a whole.
